t: Minimum Elements to Add to Form a Given Sum — One Ceiling Division Away
o:
## Understanding the problem

Every element of nums satisfies |nums[i]| <= limit, and we may append any number of new elements under the same bound until the total equals goal. Each appended element shifts the sum by at most limit in either direction, so the whole task is about closing the gap d = goal − sum(nums) using steps of magnitude at most limit — greedily, full-size ±limit steps until one final smaller step finishes the job.

**Example walkthrough:** nums = [1,−1,1] sums to 1 and goal = −4, leaving a gap of 5. With limit = 3, one element covers at most 3, so two are needed — add −3 and −2 — giving the answer 2. In the second example the sum is 1, goal is 0, so a single −1 closes the gap of 1 and the answer is 1.

Constraints matter mostly for arithmetic: with up to 10⁵ elements of magnitude up to 10⁶, |sum| approaches 10¹¹, so the gap can reach ~1.01·10¹¹ — beyond 32-bit integers in Java/C++, and far too many iterations to simulate one element at a time. We need reasoning that runs in a single pass.
k: Normalize first: only the gap d = goal − sum(nums) matters; the internal composition of the array is irrelevant.
Each append moves the sum by at most limit, so the minimum count is exactly ⌈|d| / limit⌉ — full-size greedy steps are optimal because order and signs are unrestricted.
|sum| can reach 10^11 (10^5 elements × 10^6 bound), so 64-bit accumulation is mandatory in Java/C++; JavaScript doubles stay exact below 2^53.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy simulation — peel off limit-sized steps
a.i: Simulate the greedy literally: repeatedly shave a limit-sized chunk off the remaining gap, counting one appended element per chunk. This makes the ceiling structure visible and is easy to justify — any solution needs at least ⌈|gap|/limit⌉ elements because each covers at most limit of the gap. But it is pseudo-polynomial: with limit = 1 and a gap near 10^11 the loop spins ~10^11 times, so it cannot pass the largest tests.
s: Compute the absolute gap diff = |goal − sum(nums)| using a wide accumulator.
While diff > 0, subtract limit from diff and increment steps.
a.t: O(|goal − Σnums| / limit) — one loop turn per appended element; up to ~10^11 iterations in the worst case (TLE)

a.i: Replace the loop with arithmetic. The answer is exactly ⌈diff / limit⌉, and integer ceiling division (diff + limit − 1) / limit avoids floating-point rounding entirely. One pass sums the array — in 64-bit! — and one expression finishes. Nothing faster exists, since every element must be read to know the sum.
s: Set diff = |goal − sum| as a 64-bit value.
Return (diff + limit − 1) / limit using integer division.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to compute the sum; the formula itself is O(1)

w:
## Wrap-up

Go straight to the gap argument: offset the goal by the current sum, argue each element covers at most limit of the gap, conclude ceiling division. Mention the simulation only as motivation for the formula.

**Common pitfalls**

- Overflow: 10^5 elements of magnitude 10^6 overflow int32 in Java/C++; accumulate in long / long long before taking abs.
- Floating-point ceilings invite rounding bugs at 10^11-scale numerators; the integer idiom (diff + limit − 1) / limit is bulletproof.
- diff = 0 must yield 0 — the formula handles it since (limit − 1) / limit = 0, but hand-rolled branches often forget.
- Appended elements obey the same |value| <= limit rule; that restriction is exactly why the answer is a ceiling rather than one giant element.

**Likely follow-ups:** what if appended elements must be positive, must be distinct, or limit could be 0 (then only diff = 0 is achievable)?
